WHAT COUNTS AS PAYMENT FOR AN OWNERSHIP STAKE — CONSIDERATION FOR CORPORATE SHARES AND CONTRIBUTIONS TO AN LLC, LIMITED PARTNERSHIP, OR GENERAL PARTNERSHIP (CORP. CODE §§ 152, 408–412, 15905.01–15905.02, 16401, 17704.01–17704.03, 25110; LAB. CODE §§ 406–407) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Harbor Lane Coffee, Inc. · California corporation; California LLC; California limited partnership

PURPOSE AND SCOPE — WHAT CALIFORNIA LAW ACCEPTS AS PAYMENT FOR AN OWNERSHIP STAKE
This information sheet concerns the ownership interest in Harbor Lane Coffee, Inc., a California corporation; California LLC; California limited partnership, that is to be or has been issued to Dana Ruiz on or about March 4, 2026 in exchange for $10,000 in cash; a promissory note; design work already performed. It sets out what California statutes say about what may be given in exchange for an ownership stake in a business entity, and what the same statutes say cannot count: the list of permitted consideration for corporate shares in Corporations Code section 409(a)(1) and that subdivision’s exclusion of the purchaser’s own promissory notes and of future services; the employee and director stock purchase and option plan provisions of section 408, which permit a corporation to aid those persons in paying for shares by compensation for services rendered, promissory notes or otherwise; Labor Code sections 406 and 407, which treat property put up by an employee or applicant as a bond and declare the sale of stock or an interest in a business in connection with securing a position illegal as against the public policy of the state, and the carve-outs from those sections in Corporations Code sections 408(c) and 17704.01(e); the board’s valuation role and the “fully paid” consequence in section 409(b) and (e); the timing rule in section 410(b) and the partly paid share mechanism in section 409(d); the liability of subscribers, original issuees, and transferees for unpaid consideration in sections 410(a), 411, and 412; the shareholders’ role where the articles reserve it under section 409(c) and the vote that section 152 defines; the far broader list of permitted contributions to a limited liability company in section 17704.02 and to a limited partnership in section 15905.01, together with the enforcement provisions in sections 17704.03 and 15905.02; the absence of any comparable restriction in the general partnership statute and the default rules of section 16401; and the separate qualification requirement that Corporations Code section 25110 imposes on the offer or sale of a security in an issuer transaction. What Dana Ruiz is actually giving, what it is worth, whether the entity’s board or members have acted, and whether any of these sections applies to this particular transaction are questions this sheet does not answer. Naming a person, a date, and a described payment here does not establish that any rule below governs this transaction; this sheet states what the statutes say rather than advising anyone what to do about a particular issuance, contribution, or dispute.

WHAT A CALIFORNIA CORPORATION MAY ACCEPT FOR ITS SHARES, AND WHO FIXES THE AMOUNT
The General Corporation Law lists, in one subdivision, what a California corporation may receive in exchange for issuing its shares. Corporations Code section 409(a)(1) says shares may be issued for such consideration as is determined from time to time by the board — or by the shareholders if the articles so provide — consisting of any or all of five categories: money paid; labor done; services actually rendered to the corporation or for its benefit or in its formation or reorganization; debts or securities canceled; and tangible or intangible property actually received either by the issuing corporation or by a wholly owned subsidiary.

Two features of that list are visible on its face. First, the decision about how much consideration a share is issued for is the board’s, unless the articles give it to the shareholders. Second, the categories are backward-looking in their wording: services must have been “actually rendered,” property must have been “actually received,” and debts or securities must have been “canceled.” Section 409(a)(2) separately allows shares to be issued without new consideration in the mechanical transactions it lists — a share dividend, a stock split or reverse split, a reclassification, conversion, or exchange of outstanding shares into or for shares of another class, or other change affecting outstanding shares.

TWO THINGS THE STATUTE SAYS ARE NOT PAYMENT FOR CORPORATE SHARES: THE PURCHASER’S PROMISSORY NOTE AND FUTURE SERVICES
The same subdivision that lists what a corporation may accept ends with an exclusion. Corporations Code section 409(a)(1) states that neither promissory notes of the purchaser nor future services shall constitute payment or part payment for shares of the corporation. The exclusion of the purchaser’s note carries two parenthetical exceptions written into the statute itself: a note may count if it is adequately secured by collateral other than the shares acquired, or if it is permitted by section 408, the employee and director stock plan section addressed in the next clause.

The words of the exclusion are narrow in one direction and broad in another. It reaches “promissory notes of the purchaser” — the buyer’s own note — rather than every note, and collateral consisting of the very shares being bought does not satisfy the exception. On the other side, the exclusion of “future services” has no stated exception at all apart from what section 408 permits, and it stands alongside the list’s inclusion of “labor done” and “services actually rendered”: work already performed for the corporation or in its formation is inside the list of permitted consideration, while a promise of work to come is placed outside it.

THE STATUTORY EXCEPTION: EMPLOYEE AND DIRECTOR STOCK PURCHASE AND OPTION PLANS UNDER SECTION 408
Corporations Code section 408 is the provision section 409 points to when it allows a purchaser’s promissory note to count. Section 408(a) says a corporation may adopt and carry out a stock purchase plan or agreement, or a stock option plan or agreement, providing for the issue and sale of its unissued shares, or of issued shares acquired or to be acquired, to one or more of the employees or directors of the corporation or of a subsidiary or parent, or to a trustee on their behalf, for such consideration as may be fixed and for payment in installments or at one time; and the same subdivision says the corporation may provide for aiding any such persons in paying for the shares by compensation for services rendered, promissory notes or otherwise.

Section 408(b) lists features such a plan or agreement may include, among them eligibility for participation, the class and price of shares, the number of shares that may be subscribed for, the method of payment, the reservation of title until full payment, the effect of termination of employment, an option or obligation on the corporation’s part to repurchase the shares on termination of employment, restrictions on transfer of the shares, and the time limits and termination of the plan. The subdivision states these as permitted contents, not as requirements.

THE LABOR CODE RULE ABOUT BUYING INTO A BUSINESS TO GET A JOB, AND THE CARVE-OUTS FOR PLAN SHARES AND LLC INTERESTS
Two Labor Code sections sit next to these corporate provisions. Labor Code section 406 says any property put up by an employee, or applicant, as a part of the contract of employment, directly or indirectly, is deemed to be put up as a bond subject to that article, whether the property is put up on a note or as a loan or an investment and regardless of the wording of the agreement under which it is put up. Labor Code section 407 states that investments and the sale of stock or an interest in a business in connection with the securing of a position are illegal as against the public policy of the state and shall not be advertised or held out in any way as a part of the consideration for any employment.

The Corporations Code then carves specific transactions out of those two sections. Section 408(c) says Labor Code sections 406 and 407 do not apply to shares issued by a foreign or domestic corporation to an employee of the corporation or of a parent or subsidiary under a stock purchase or stock option plan or agreement of the kind described in section 408(a), or, in any transaction in connection with securing employment, to a person who is or is about to become an officer of the corporation or of a parent or subsidiary. Section 17704.01(e) makes the parallel carve-out for membership interests issued by a limited liability company or foreign limited liability company to an employee under a membership interest purchase or option plan or agreement, and, in a transaction in connection with securing employment, to a person who is or is about to become an officer or a manager.

VALUING NON-CASH CONSIDERATION: THE BOARD’S RESOLUTION, AND WHEN SHARES ARE “FULLY PAID”
Corporations Code section 409 assigns the valuation of non-cash consideration to the board and states the consequence of a valid issuance. Section 409(e) says the board shall state by resolution its determination of the fair value to the corporation, in monetary terms, of any consideration other than money for which shares are issued, and adds that the subdivision does not affect the accounting treatment of the transaction, which is to conform to generally accepted accounting principles. The obligation is phrased as a duty of the board (“shall state by resolution”) rather than as a filing with any public office.

Section 409(b) states the effect of an issuance made as that section or section 408 provides: except for partly paid shares issued under section 409(d), the shares are declared and taken to be fully paid stock, not liable to any further call, and the holder is not liable for any further payments under the General Corporation Law. The same subdivision adds that, in the absence of fraud in the transaction, the judgment of the directors as to the value of the consideration for shares is conclusive.

WHEN THE CONSIDERATION MUST BE PAID, AND THE STATUTORY ROUTE FOR SHARES THAT ARE NOT FULLY PAID
Corporations Code section 410(b) fixes the timing: the full agreed consideration for shares shall be paid prior to or concurrently with the issuance, unless the shares are issued as partly paid under section 409(d), in which case the consideration is paid in accordance with the agreement of subscription or purchase. Payment on a schedule is therefore not outside the statute; it is inside a specific mechanism the statute provides.

Section 409(d) describes that mechanism. A corporation may issue the whole or any part of its shares as partly paid and subject to call for the remainder of the consideration. The certificate representing partly paid shares — or, for uncertificated securities, the initial transaction statement — must state the total amount of the consideration to be paid and the amount paid on it. And when a dividend is declared on fully paid shares, the corporation must declare a dividend on partly paid shares of the same class, but only on the basis of the percentage of the consideration actually paid.

WHO OWES THE CORPORATION FOR CONSIDERATION THAT WAS NEVER PAID: SUBSCRIBERS, ORIGINAL ISSUEES, AND LATER HOLDERS
Corporations Code section 410(a) states the basic obligation: every subscriber to shares and every person to whom shares are originally issued is liable to the corporation for the full consideration agreed to be paid for the shares. The liability runs to the corporation and attaches to the person who subscribed or to whom the shares were first issued.

Sections 411 and 412 address people who acquire such shares afterward. Under section 411, a transferee of shares for which the full agreed consideration has not been paid, who acquired them in good faith and without knowledge that they were not paid in full or to the extent stated on the certificate or initial transaction statement, is liable only for the amount shown by that certificate or statement to be unpaid, until the transferee transfers the shares to someone who becomes liable; the transferor remains personally liable if the certificate or statement so provides or if that was agreed in writing, and a later holder who takes title through such a transferee and is not a party to any fraud affecting the issue has the same liability as the transferee through whom title came. Section 412 addresses partly paid shares specifically: a transferee who acquired them under a certificate or initial transaction statement showing the fact of part payment, and a transferee who acquired them with actual knowledge that the full agreed consideration had not been paid to the extent stated — other than one who derives title through a good faith holder without knowledge and who is not a party to any fraud affecting the issue — is personally liable to the corporation for installments becoming due until the shares are transferred to someone who becomes liable, with the same proviso about a transferor who remains personally liable.

WHEN THE ARTICLES GIVE THE CONSIDERATION DECISION TO THE SHAREHOLDERS INSTEAD OF THE BOARD
Section 409(a)(1) leaves the consideration decision with the board “or by the shareholders if the articles so provide,” and section 409(c) supplies the mechanism for that alternative: if the articles reserve to the shareholders the right to determine the consideration for the issue of any shares, that determination is made by approval of the outstanding shares, with a parenthetical pointing to section 152.

Section 152 defines that phrase for the General Corporation Law. “Approved by (or approval of) the outstanding shares” means approved by the affirmative vote of a majority of the outstanding shares entitled to vote; the approval must include the affirmative vote of a majority of the outstanding shares of each class or series entitled by the articles or by the General Corporation Law to vote as a class or series on the subject matter, and must also include the affirmative vote of any greater proportion, including all, of the outstanding shares of a class or series where the articles or that division require a greater proportion.

THE LLC RULE IS WRITTEN THE OTHER WAY: PROMISSORY NOTES, SERVICES PERFORMED, AND CONTRACTS FOR SERVICES TO BE PERFORMED
The California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act takes the opposite drafting approach to the corporate statute. Corporations Code section 17704.02 says a contribution may consist of tangible or intangible property or other benefit to a limited liability company, including money, services performed, promissory notes, other agreements to contribute money or property, and contracts for services to be performed. The two items the corporate statute expressly excludes — the purchaser’s promissory note and future services — appear in the LLC statute’s list of what a contribution may consist of.

The same act also states that a contribution is not a precondition of membership at all: section 17704.01(d) says a person may become a member without acquiring a transferable interest and without making or being obligated to make a contribution to the limited liability company.

THE GENERAL PARTNERSHIP STATUTE SAYS NOTHING ABOUT WHAT A PARTNER MUST CONTRIBUTE

Corporations Code section 410(b) fixes the timing: the full agreed consideration for shares shall be paid prior to or concurrently with the issuance, unless the shares are issued as partly paid under section 409(d), in which case the consideration is paid in accordance with the agreement of subscription or purchase. Payment on a schedule is therefore not outside the statute; it is inside a specific mechanism the statute provides.

Section 409(d) describes that mechanism. A corporation may issue the whole or any part of its shares as partly paid and subject to call for the remainder of the consideration. The certificate representing partly paid shares — or, for uncertificated securities, the initial transaction statement — must state the total amount of the consideration to be paid and the amount paid on it. And when a dividend is declared on fully paid shares, the corporation must declare a dividend on partly paid shares of the same class, but only on the basis of the percentage of the consideration actually paid.

Corporations Code section 410(a) states the basic obligation: every subscriber to shares and every person to whom shares are originally issued is liable to the corporation for the full consideration agreed to be paid for the shares. The liability runs to the corporation and attaches to the person who subscribed or to whom the shares were first issued.

Sections 411 and 412 address people who acquire such shares afterward. Under section 411, a transferee of shares for which the full agreed consideration has not been paid, who acquired them in good faith and without knowledge that they were not paid in full or to the extent stated on the certificate or initial transaction statement, is liable only for the amount shown by that certificate or statement to be unpaid, until the transferee transfers the shares to someone who becomes liable; the transferor remains personally liable if the certificate or statement so provides or if that was agreed in writing, and a later holder who takes title through such a transferee and is not a party to any fraud affecting the issue has the same liability as the transferee through whom title came. Section 412 addresses partly paid shares specifically: a transferee who acquired them under a certificate or initial transaction statement showing the fact of part payment, and a transferee who acquired them with actual knowledge that the full agreed consideration had not been paid to the extent stated — other than one who derives title through a good faith holder without knowledge and who is not a party to any fraud affecting the issue — is personally liable to the corporation for installments becoming due until the shares are transferred to someone who becomes liable, with the same proviso about a transferor who remains personally liable.

Because a limited liability company may take a promise as a contribution, the act states what happens when the promise is not kept. Corporations Code section 17704.03(a) says a person’s obligation to make a contribution is not excused by the person’s death, disability, or other inability to perform personally, and that if a person does not make a required contribution, that person or the person’s estate is obligated to contribute money equal to the value of the part of the contribution that has not been made, at the option of the limited liability company.
